title: Uhud: the archers
hookLine: the archers are told not to leave their hill, even if they see birds snatching the army; they leave for the spoils, and the victory turns (3:152; Bukhari)

lines: EVEN IF YOU SEE BIRDS SNATCHING US.
cards: Even if you see birds snatching us, don't leave this place until I send for you. That's the order, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in close paraphrase.
The Meccans have come back after Badr, to the foot of a mountain outside Medina called Uhud.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ places a company of archers on a small hill, under a companion named Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the army's back. The order couldn't be clearer. Whatever you see, stay.

teach.b: At first, the battle goes the Muslims' way. In Bukhari's report, the Meccan line breaks and starts to run. From the hill, the archers can see it: the enemy fleeing, the camp left behind, everything there for the taking.
Some start calling out: the spoils, the spoils! Your companions have won, what are you waiting for?

teach.h: HAVE YOU FORGOTTEN WHAT HE TOLD YOU?
teach.b: Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? They answer that they'll go down to the people and take their share. And they go.
The hill is left nearly empty, and the battle turns. Muslims are killed, and the Prophet himself is wounded. Surah Al Imran tells this moment without softening it.

Allah kept His promise to you, the verse says, when you were driving them back, until your courage failed, and you argued about the order, and you disobeyed, after He had shown you what you longed for.
Then a short line that names the whole thing, in Pickthall's words: "Some of you desired the world, and some of you desired the Hereafter." The verse doesn't name names.
It says some, and some, in one army, on one afternoon. And then it does something surprising: it says Allah has forgiven them.
Some Muslim teachers tell Uhud to name a very ordinary temptation: leaving your post a little early, because the reward is right there and the work looks finished.

how: Muslims read the Uhud passage of Surah Al Imran as a lesson in obedience and forgiveness, and the story of the archers is a common theme in sermons and sirah classes.

o: the mountain near Medina where a won battle turned
the valley where Mecca's caravans rested at night
a hill near Mecca where pilgrims gather to pray

p: commander of the archers on the hill
even if you see birds snatching us

s: the archers were told they could leave once the enemy ran
the order was: even if you see birds snatching us, don't leave until I send for you.
Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminded them of the order
he asked: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you?
the Qur'an ends the account with a curse on the archers
after naming what went wrong, it says Allah has forgiven them.

games.q: you're Abdullah ibn Jubayr, in charge of the archers. the enemy is running, and your men start down the hill toward the spoils. what do you do?
o: go down with them; the battle's won.
remind them of the Prophet's order.
leave the hill to ask the Prophet what to do.
games.why: he asked them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? they went down anyway, and the battle turned.

practice: Think of one place you've been asked to hold a post, a child you're watching, a shift, a promise someone is counting on, and notice the pull toward the valley: the phone, the reward, calling it done before it is.
Don't fight it; just see it clearly, the way the archers saw the spoils, and stay on the hill one breath longer. If you pray, you can ask Allah for steadiness.

wordCard.voice: Uhud: the mountain outside Medina where a victory turned, after archers left their hill for the spoils, and the verse that named it and forgave them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name of the mountain outside Medina where the battle was fought.

carryVoice: Your line: stay on the hill. The verse that named the failure also forgave it. That's day seven hundred seventy-nine.
